title: Australian national security culture is founded on the interaction of three factors: fear, self-delusion and status seeking.
text:
Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

Since the announcement of AUKUS in September 2021, I have been a frequent critic. I couldn’t see any rational explanation for its undertaking or any benefit that would make Australia more secure. In return for a vast expenditure of taxpayers’ dollars, Australia’s leaders decided to accept much greater risk to the nation – up to and including nuclear annihilation – without any tangible gain. They did so on the basis of the distant and possible non-arrival of promised nuclear-powered submarines.

Then I had a revelation. My approach until now had been to examine AUKUS through a national security lens. This was a mistake. I had wrongly assumed the government used the same methodology and in doing so I had failed to consider the cognitive limits of our political leaders. What I had not realised was that the government’s approach to national security has an overwhelming cultural bias, whose origins date to the establishment of the nation in 1901.

The enthusiasm of the Australian political class for AUKUS is founded on values that were codified at Federation and have underpinned national security decision-making ever since. AUKUS represents not so much a response to a security threat – Australia remains among the safest countries in the world – but rather the veneration of a longstanding cultural tradition.

This realisation does nothing to persuade me AUKUS is a good deal for the country, but at least I now understand how something so patently foolish came to be so easily accepted and vigorously defended by members of our political class. I now understand how the leaders of both the Labor and Coalition political parties have so easily wedded themselves to the same policy and have done so with minimal consultation, even with their backbenchers, let alone members of the public.

Australian national security culture is founded on the interaction of three factors: fear, self-delusion and status seeking. All date from the Federation of the nation in 1901 and have steered security decision-making for 125 years. I will take each one in turn.

Fear is Australia’s founding emotion. The nation’s history has witnessed numerous invasion scares in which a foreign power was supposedly poised to take over the country. Candidates for Australia’s potential overlord included France, Russia, Japan, China and even the United States. These scares all lacked any basis in reality. Our continent’s immutable geography has always made it among the safest places in the world. The only invasion it has known was the one that began in 1788 with the arrival of the First Fleet and its convict settlers.

Australian governments have always accepted as fact two unproven propositions – the possibility of invasion and the nation’s inability to defend itself. Consequently Australia has always relied on a great power protector for its security.

This fear of invasion masked an even greater terror that dominated the focus of the nation’s first leaders ­– the fear of the “yellow peril” from the north. Asia’s proximity caused many Australians to fear being overwhelmed by the mass arrival of migrants from there. In 1901, this fear was laid out in the most plain, direct and racist terms in the nation’s first parliament. Parliamentarians held nothing back as they debated and approved the Immigration Restriction Act, the foundational legislation of the White Australia policy.

Fear of Chinese and other Asian migrants taking over the country flowed into the second cultural factor that underpins Australia’s construction of national security, which is self-delusion. Australian governments have always accepted as fact two unproven propositions – the possibility of invasion, as noted above, and the nation’s inability to defend itself. Consequently Australia has always relied on a great power protector for its security. First it was the United Kingdom and now it is the US.

At Federation, Australia lacked the population, industrial development and wealth to defend itself against a major power, so handing national security to London was the best option. However, these weaknesses are no longer applicable. Australia is a modern, wealthy state with an educated population and has the enormous defensive benefit of possessing no land borders. Moreover, modern military technologies such as long-range precision missiles and drones, coupled with ubiquitous sensors, favour the defender.

So embedded has been this faith in a great power coming to Australia’s aid that even the failure of the Singapore Strategy in World War II has done nothing to deter subsequent government leaders from embracing it. All that happened was that we changed friends, not our beliefs or expectations.

The final factor is Australia’s continuing aspiration for a higher status in the ranking of the world’s nations than it would naturally deserve on its own. Australia claims to be a middle power, but the reality is that in the distribution of power only great states matter. Despite its vast natural resources, Australia lacks the population and industrial base to achieve great power status.

There is a substitute for power in our own right, however – the chance to bask in the reflected glory of more important friends. Clinton Fernandes, a professor of international and political studies at UNSW Canberra, hit the bullseye when he wrote of “sub-imperial power” to describe Australia’s ambition and place in the world.

Australia positions itself within the aura of a great power and thereby bestows upon itself the same place in the world, although this is not done without cost. When the protector was the UK, this positioning was a reflection of its place in the British Empire. As Britain’s status declined, Australia sought a new place to shelter and became an unofficial member of the American empire. When George W. Bush called John Howard his “sheriff” the term encompassed more than just a passing reference to Australia’s role in the region. It was a recognition of Australia’s position in the global order.

Australian leaders consider maintaining the relationship with the US to be their most vital defence responsibility. They pretend not to notice when the US starts an illegal war, threatens allies or implements a vindictive tariff policy. The equanimity with which Richard Marles received the US decision that Australia would only receive three second-hand submarines rather than two used and one new highlights the government’s inability to question Washington, despite being the victim of a bait and switch. The earlier desperation with which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pursued a meeting with President Donald Trump and finally settled for a photo-op might be seen by many as an embarrassment. For the prime minister, it was policy.

The decisive role of this institutional mindset in Australian national security deliberations points to the challenge of making a change. There is a saying among those who think about strategy: culture eats strategy for breakfast. Australia demonstrates the insightfulness of those words.

Culture is always a factor in strategy-making, and it should be. How a people see themselves must play a part in a country’s deliberations on the way it approaches security. Yet entrenched culture must not be prioritised at the expense of other factors, as is being done in Australia. Geography, psychology and a realistic assessment of the threat environment must be accorded a high degree of influence.

Our perception of insecurity and our desire for global status dominate security decision-making. Moreover, these are cultural factors that were cemented in a bygone age. As the world has evolved and as Australia has changed, our political class has failed to keep pace and remains mired in an outdated mindset.

This can be read in government defence policy papers. Typically, they include a statement to the effect that the world is becoming more dangerous and unpredictable and is witnessing intense strategic competition. Invariably, the solution is to intensify the relationship with our protector, the US. Despite admitting to a changing security environment, the government’s solution is more of the same. AUKUS and a continued policy of dependence is the outcome.

Climate change, the growth of Chinese power, increasing irrationality in the US and the undermining of the global rules-based order all suggest the context for decision-making warrants something new. Yet the emergence of new problems is met with the same fear, self-delusion and desire to remain under the care of a protector.

After 125 years of this, the actions of our political leaders are testament to the difficulty of changing culture. However, Australia desperately needs to do so. It needs to accept the futility of remaining in a world shaped by the values of 1901.

AUKUS does make a perverse kind of sense, in that it is not an aberration but the extension of past practice. Any consideration of other and better options is simply not possible within the current cultural perspective. AUKUS’s validation rests on the founding ethos of an insecure nation. It is perpetuated by a present leadership that is unable to escape the limitations of the past.

Australia’s leaders could overcome the cultural bias that they bring to national security, but so far they have shown little interest in doing so. Leaders, by definition, are meant to lead. In this case, they are simply following a century of political predecessors.

Until this cultural baggage is dealt with, and governments begin making decisions based on contemporary realities and actual defence needs, AUKUS will stay.

Albert Palazzo is an adjunct professor at UNSW Canberra.
